metadata.title: Unravelling the link between non-voting and political knowledge: An exploratory study

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study does not use ICCS microdata for statistical estimation; it is based on qualitative focus group discussions with non-voters in two German cases (Duisburg municipal elections 2020 and North Rhine-Westphalia state elections 2022). Because the analysis is qualitative content analysis of transcripts (coded by two coders with intercoder reliability reported via Cohen’s Kappa), there is no complex survey sampling design, no plausible-value (PV) scaling, and no survey weight variable to apply. The recruitment followed a theoretical sampling approach to reflect variation in socioeconomic and demographic characteristics, but the paper does not describe any probability sampling weights. Therefore, weighting is not part of the analytic strategy; findings are interpreted as exploratory insights into political knowledge deficits and typologies of passive citizens rather than population-representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent outcomes are not cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA scaling model; instead, the study uses qualitative focus group statements coded into typologies (disillusioned, unengaged, standby) and related themes about political knowledge and abstention. Missing-data handling is not reported because the dataset is composed of anonymized focus group transcripts and coded qualitative content; there is no item-level missingness mechanism analogous to survey questionnaires with PV-based achievement scales. As a result, the paper does not document a quantitative missing-data procedure.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses qualitative focus group data rather than ILSA student microdata. Participants were recruited to represent non-voters for (a) Duisburg municipal elections in 2020 and (b) North Rhine-Westphalia state elections in 2022. Recruitment used a theoretical sampling model to reflect variation in socioeconomic and demographic characteristics; an opinion research institute conducted recruitment (e.g., phone calls) and obtained informed consent. Duisburg: five online Zoom focus groups with 27 participants in September 2021. North Rhine-Westphalia: eight online Zoom focus groups with 52 participants conducted between March and May 2023. The paper reports that groups were kept to four to seven participants and that participants varied in gender, age, profession, and migration background; two Duisburg groups and four NRW groups included participants with at least university-entrance-level qualifications, while other groups included participants with lower formal education. Data were generated via recorded and transcribed discussions and then analyzed via qualitative content analysis in MAXQDA with separate coding per discussion by two coders.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This paper is an exploratory qualitative study addressing how political knowledge relates to non-voting, using focus group discussions rather than quantitative ILSA microdata analysis. The empirical material comes from two German cases: non-voters in Duisburg’s 2020 municipal elections (five focus groups, 27 participants) and non-voters in North Rhine-Westphalia’s 2022 state elections (eight focus groups, 52 participants). The authors apply and extend Amnå & Ekman’s typology of passive citizens (disillusioned, unengaged, standby) to interpret “paths to participation” and identify where political knowledge deficits occur (e.g., understanding political system functioning vs. campaign/party communication). No ML models, PV-based achievement outcomes, or survey-weighted statistical estimates are reported; instead, coded qualitative themes are used to derive implications for civic education design. Limitations include restricted age coverage (excluding first-time voters and participants older than 70) and the inherent non-representativeness of focus group sampling. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to ILSA/ML fields because the article does not conduct an empirical machine-learning prediction/classification task on ICCS (or any other ILSA) student microdata. Although ICCS is referenced as a conceptual source for political knowledge and civic education constructs, the study’s actual dataset is qualitative focus group transcripts from two German election contexts. Consequently, there are no PV-handling, missing-data procedures, survey weights, ML algorithms, or numeric predictive performance metrics to extract.
